aiGenerationNote:

Then, transition to a live coding demo (7-8 min) in IntelliJ IDEA. Walk through creating a new project, a new class, typing the "Hello, World!" code, and running it. screens.title: Introduction to Java and Your First Program
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn what makes Java widely used, how the Java runtime pieces fit together, and how to create a tiny, runnable program. Java was designed for portability: code compiled once becomes bytecode that the Java Virtual Machine can run on any supported platform. That portability is what lets the same compiled program work on Windows, Mac O S, or Linux without recompilation. You will also learn the practical tools you need: the Java Development Kit, which contains the compiler and tools, the Java Runtime Environment that bundles the runtime libraries, and the JVM that executes bytecode. Finally, we'll walk through a small example program, how to compile it with the Java compiler, and how to run the resulting bytecode on the JVM. By the end of this lesson you will understand the purpose of each core component, be able to set up an IDE and JDK, and produce and run a first program. Think about your development environment now: which operating system will you use, and what benefit of Java portability matters most to your projects?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will complete a set of practical skills that form the foundation of Java development. First, you will be able to explain Java's core principles and advantages, such as portability and robustness, with concrete examples of where that matters. Second, you will be able to install and configure a Java Development Kit and an IDE so you can write, compile, and run programs. Third, you will author a basic Java class with the correct main method signature and produce console output. And fourth, you will learn to identify and fix common compilation and runtime errors like missing semicolons, case-sensitivity mistakes, or mismatched file and class names. Each objective pairs a clear outcome with a small milestone you can verify inside your IDE or terminal. We'll guide you through each step and show the common pitfalls so you gain practical confidence, not just theory.

screens.title: What is Java and why portability matters
screens.narratorSegment: Java is a programming language created with portability, safety, and clarity as central goals. The idea is that you write human-readable Java source code, compile it into an intermediate form called bytecode, and then let a Java Virtual Machine execute that bytecode on any supported platform. This separation—source, bytecode, and runtime—gives Java its famous 'write once, run anywhere' advantage. In practice, that means a single compiled class file can be shipped to different servers or user machines without recompiling for each operating system. Typical uses include large enterprise backend systems where platform consistency matters, Android app foundations, and server-side processing. A concrete example is compiling a simple class on your laptop and running the same. class file on a Linux server with a JVM installed. A common misconception is that the JVM magically converts Java source directly into native instructions; instead, Java compiles to bytecode first, and the JVM executes or further translates that bytecode. Key takeaway: thinking in terms of bytecode and JVM execution helps you reason about compatibility and performance trade-offs. How might portability influence your choice of language for a cross-platform project?

keyIdea.title: Definition insight
keyIdea.text: Java's portability comes from compiling to JVM bytecode, not from running source directly on different machines.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What is Java
Definition
Java is a language designed to compile to bytecode that runs on a Java Virtual Machine. That bytecode is platform-neutral which enables the same compiled artifact to execute across different operating systems when a JVM is available.
Concrete example
Compile a small class on Windows to produce a .class file, then run that .class file on a Linux machine with a JVM. The output is identical without recompiling.
Common misconception
Java does not run source text directly on any platform. The compilation step to bytecode is essential for portability; the JVM executes the bytecode.
Key Takeaway

Treat bytecode as the portable artifact and the JVM as the execution environment for that artifact.

Where Java is used
Enterprise backends
Stable deployment and platform-neutral artifacts suit large systems.
Android foundations
Java concepts inform many mobile runtimes and tools.
Server-side processing
Bytecode portability eases deployment across cloud environments.

screens.title: JVM, JRE, and JDK — roles and differences
screens.narratorSegment: Java development and execution rely on three related components that are easy to confuse: the JVM, the JRE, and the JDK. The Java Virtual Machine is the abstract execution engine that reads and runs bytecode; it is the component responsible for translating or interpreting compiled Java classes into actions on the host machine. The Java Runtime Environment bundles a JVM with the standard class libraries and supporting files your application needs at runtime. The Java Development Kit is a superset of the JRE: it contains everything the JRE provides plus development tools such as the Java compiler, debugger, and utilities. A concrete way to think about this is: if you only need to run programs, install the JRE; if you must write and compile code, install the JDK. A common confusion is expecting source code to run without compiling; the compiler in the JDK produces the. class bytecode the JVM executes. Key takeaway: install a JDK during development so you have both compilation and runtime capabilities available. JVM, JRE, and JDK — roles and differences means jdk = dev tools + jre. jre = jvm + libraries. jvm = execution engine for bytecode.. In practical terms, compare the three components that make java development possible. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Quick comparison
JVM
Execution engine that runs Java bytecode on a host platform.
JRE
Includes a JVM and the standard class libraries needed at runtime.
JDK
Adds development tools such as the compiler, in addition to the JRE.
Concrete example
When learning, install the JDK. Use the included javac compiler to produce .class files, then run those files with the java command provided by the JRE/JDK.
Key Takeaway

Keep the JDK installed while developing so you have both compile-time tools and runtime pieces available.

Visual mapping
JDK
javac, debugger, tools + JRE
JRE
JVM + libraries
JVM
Executes .class bytecode
Misconception check: installing only a JRE prevents you from compiling source locally. If you see a missing javac command, you likely installed only a runtime package.

screens.title: From source to running program
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the exact steps that take your Java source to a running program. Step one is writing source code in a. java file, typically a class declaration. Step two is compiling that file using the Java compiler, which produces a. class file containing Java bytecode. The command-line flow is simple: run the compiler with the source filename and, if successful, invoke the java runtime with the class name (without the. class extension) to execute it. For example, saving MyFirstProgram. java, running the compiler, and then running java MyFirstProgram produces the console output. A concrete scenario: you type a small class with a main method, you run javac, the compiler reports either success or compilation errors; if success, you run java and the JVM executes the bytecode and shows the printed message. A common mistake is attempting to run the. java file directly with the java command. The java command runs compiled classes, not source files. Key takeaway: remember the two-step sequence—compile, then execute—and confirm that the public class name matches the filename before compiling. From source to running program means the developer compiles source into bytecode with javac, then the jvm runs the bytecode via the java command; compile errors block the second step.. In practical terms, step-by-step of writing, compiling, and executing a java program. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: The developer compiles source into bytecode with javac, then the JVM runs the bytecode via the java command; compile errors block the second step.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Source → Bytecode → JVM
Step-by-step
  1. Write a public class in a .java file with a main method.
  2. Compile with the Java compiler: javac YourClassName.java to create a .class file.
  3. Run the compiled class with the JVM: java YourClassName to execute the program.
Concrete example
Save MyFirstProgram.java, run javac MyFirstProgram.java, then run java MyFirstProgram to see printed output in the console.
Common mistake
Trying to run source with the java command directly. The java command expects compiled classes; use javac first.
Terminal commands (example)
javac MyFirstProgram.java
# produces MyFirstProgram.class
java MyFirstProgram
# runs the bytecode on the JVM
Why it matters
Understanding this two-step flow helps you diagnose whether an issue is a compile-time error or an execution problem.
Key Takeaway

Compile first with javac, then run with java; confirm class and filename alignment to avoid early failures.

screens.title: Setting up the JDK and configuring IntelliJ IDEA
screens.narratorSegment: Before writing code, you must install a JDK and configure your IDE so the compiler and runtime are available. Install a recent OpenJDK or Oracle JDK distribution and make sure your operating system PATH includes the JDK tools if you plan to use the terminal. In IntelliJ IDEA, create a new Java project and select your installed JDK; the IDE will remember this SDK for compiling and running projects. A practical example: when you create a new project in IntelliJ, the project wizard asks for the Java SDK location—point it to the JDK installation directory. If the IDE cannot find the compiler, you will not be able to run classes from the run menu. Common issues include picking only a runtime package or misconfigured SDK paths. Key takeaway: confirm your IDE sees the JDK and that javac is available on the command line if you also plan to compile outside the IDE. This small setup step saves time and reduces confusion when your first program doesn't run. Setting up the JDK and configuring IntelliJ IDEA means ensure the jdk is installed and configured in both your terminal path and your ide so compilation and execution are available.. In practical terms, install the development kit and point your ide to it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Installation checklist

screens.title: Create a new project and Java class in IntelliJ
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through creating a new project and adding a Java class inside IntelliJ. Start the IDE, choose New Project, pick Java, and ensure the SDK points to your installed JDK. Create the project with a src folder visible in the Project view. Right-click src, choose New → Java Class, and enter a class name such as Greetings. The IDE will create a file named Greetings. java containing the class declaration. A concrete example: create Greetings. java and add a main method inside it. Remember that Java is case-sensitive and that the public class name should match the filename exactly; if the class is public and called Greetings, the file must be Greetings. java. IntelliJ helps by offering code completion and immediate highlighting of issues. A common misconception is that the filename can differ from the public class name; this causes a compilation error. Key takeaway: use the IDE project structure and naming conventions to avoid avoidable compile-time errors. Create a new project and Java class in IntelliJ means when creating a public class, name the file exactly the same as the public class to prevent compiler errors.. Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Create Project & Class
Quick steps in IntelliJ
  1. Select New Project → Java and pick the SDK.
  2. Finish the wizard and open the Project view.
  3. Right-click src → New → Java Class and name it exactly.
Concrete example file
// Greetings.java
public class Greetings {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    // TODO: add console output
  }
}
Naming pitfall
If your public class name and filename differ, javac will report an error preventing compilation.
IDE support
IntelliJ highlights syntax problems as you type and provides a Run action. Use the Project view to confirm the file is in src and named correctly.
Try this
Create Greetings.java, add a main method, and run it. Observe how the IDE presents errors if the name is incorrect.
Key Takeaway

Use the IDE to enforce project structure and naming so compilation problems are fewer and easier to fix.

screens.title: Anatomy of a Java class and the main method
screens.narratorSegment: The main method serves as the entry point for standalone Java applications. Its exact signature matters because the JVM looks for a method with that name and modifiers to begin execution. 'public' makes the method accessible to the JVM from outside the class. 'static' means the method belongs to the class itself and can be called without creating an object instance. 'void' indicates the method does not return a value to the caller. The parameter list 'String[] args' accepts command-line arguments as an array of strings. A concrete example is using args to accept simple inputs: if you pass a value on the command line, the program can read it through the args array. A frequent misconception is that any method named main will be used; the JVM requires the exact signature. If your method differs, the compiler may accept it but the JVM will not find an appropriate entry point. Key takeaway: write the exact main signature to ensure the JVM starts your application correctly and use the args array when you want basic command-line input. Anatomy of a Java class and the main method means the jvm looks for a public static void main(string[] args) method as the application entry point; any deviation prevents automatic execution.. In practical terms, understand each part of public static void main(string[] args). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Class & main
Breakdown of the signature
  • public — accessible to the JVM at runtime.
  • static — belongs to the class, no object required.
  • void — no value returned to the caller.
  • String[] args — receives command-line arguments as strings.
Concrete example
If you run java MyProgram Hello, args[0] will contain "Hello" and you can use it to customize output.
Misconception
A method named main with different modifiers or parameters will not be discovered as the entry point by the JVM.
Example usage
public class MyProgram {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    if (args.length > 0) {
      System.out.println("Argument: " + args[0]);
    } else {
      System.out.println("No arguments provided.");
    }
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Write the exact main signature and use args when you need simple input from the command line.

screens.title: Common compilation errors and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often see compilation errors that are easy to repair once you know what to look for. The most common issues include missing semicolons at the end of statements, incorrect capitalization—since Java is case-sensitive—and mismatched file and public class names. For example, if you declare public class MyProgram but save the file as myprogram. java, the compiler will complain because the public class name must match the filename exactly. Another frequent source of errors is misspelling built-in identifiers like System or println; the compiler will report an unknown symbol. IntelliJ's editor highlights the offending lines and offers suggestions, but reading the compiler message is the reliable first step: it specifies the file and line number. A concrete troubleshooting workflow: read the error message, open the indicated line, check for syntax or naming problems, fix, and recompile. Key takeaway: compiler messages are your friend; use them to locate and correct the exact source of syntax or naming errors. screens.title: Runtime errors and using the IDE debugger
screens.narratorSegment: Runtime errors occur after successful compilation when the JVM executes bytecode. Examples include exceptions such as null pointer access or array index errors; these are not caught by the compiler because they're about program state at runtime. When you encounter a runtime exception, read the stack trace in the console: it tells you the exception type and the exact line where the error occurred. Use IntelliJ's debugger to set breakpoints and inspect variable values at runtime, which helps you understand why a variable is null or why an index is out of bounds. A concrete debug workflow: reproduce the error, open the stack trace to find the failing line, set a breakpoint before that line, run in debug mode, and step through to observe state changes. A common misconception is that a program that compiles is guaranteed to run; compilation only ensures syntactic correctness. Key takeaway: combine stack traces and IDE debugging tools to identify and resolve runtime issues efficiently. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn what makes Java widely used, how the Java runtime pieces fit together, and how to create a tiny, runnable program. Java was designed for portability: code compiled once becomes bytecode that the Java Virtual Machine can run on any supported platform. That portability is what lets the same compiled program work on Windows, Mac O S, or Linux without recompilation. You will also learn the practical tools you need: the Java Development Kit, which contains the compiler and tools, the Java Runtime Environment that bundles the runtime libraries, and the JVM that executes bytecode. Finally, we'll walk through a small example program, how to compile it with the Java compiler, and how to run the resulting bytecode on the JVM. By the end of this lesson you will understand the purpose of each core component, be able to set up an IDE and JDK, and produce and run a first program. Think about your development environment now: which operating system will you use, and what benefit of Java portability matters most to your projects?

By the end of this chapter you will complete a set of practical skills that form the foundation of Java development. First, you will be able to explain Java's core principles and advantages, such as portability and robustness, with concrete examples of where that matters. Second, you will be able to install and configure a Java Development Kit and an IDE so you can write, compile, and run programs. Third, you will author a basic Java class with the correct main method signature and produce console output. And fourth, you will learn to identify and fix common compilation and runtime errors like missing semicolons, case-sensitivity mistakes, or mismatched file and class names. Each objective pairs a clear outcome with a small milestone you can verify inside your IDE or terminal. We'll guide you through each step and show the common pitfalls so you gain practical confidence, not just theory.

These additional objective cards translate conceptual goals into hands-on milestones you can validate. One milestone is creating a new Java project and adding a class named exactly as the file. Another milestone is compiling and running the program from the terminal using the Java compiler and runtime commands. A third milestone is using IntelliJ IDEA's run console to execute a class and observe output, which shows the IDE provides helpful feedback and error highlighting. Finally, you will complete a short challenge to modify a starter program to print your name on a new line. Each task reinforces the same underlying ideas: class structure, the main entry point, compilation into bytecode, and execution on a JVM. These practice steps build muscle memory and reduce simple, recurring mistakes while giving you a working project you can extend.

Java is a programming language created with portability, safety, and clarity as central goals. The idea is that you write human-readable Java source code, compile it into an intermediate form called bytecode, and then let a Java Virtual Machine execute that bytecode on any supported platform. This separation—source, bytecode, and runtime—gives Java its famous 'write once, run anywhere' advantage. In practice, that means a single compiled class file can be shipped to different servers or user machines without recompiling for each operating system. Typical uses include large enterprise backend systems where platform consistency matters, Android app foundations, and server-side processing. A concrete example is compiling a simple class on your laptop and running the same. class file on a Linux server with a JVM installed. A common misconception is that the JVM magically converts Java source directly into native instructions; instead, Java compiles to bytecode first, and the JVM executes or further translates that bytecode. Key takeaway: thinking in terms of bytecode and JVM execution helps you reason about compatibility and performance trade-offs. How might portability influence your choice of language for a cross-platform project?

Java development and execution rely on three related components that are easy to confuse: the JVM, the JRE, and the JDK. The Java Virtual Machine is the abstract execution engine that reads and runs bytecode; it is the component responsible for translating or interpreting compiled Java classes into actions on the host machine. The Java Runtime Environment bundles a JVM with the standard class libraries and supporting files your application needs at runtime. The Java Development Kit is a superset of the JRE: it contains everything the JRE provides plus development tools such as the Java compiler, debugger, and utilities. A concrete way to think about this is: if you only need to run programs, install the JRE; if you must write and compile code, install the JDK. A common confusion is expecting source code to run without compiling; the compiler in the JDK produces the. class bytecode the JVM executes. Key takeaway: install a JDK during development so you have both compilation and runtime capabilities available. JVM, JRE, and JDK — roles and differences means jdk = dev tools + jre. jre = jvm + libraries. jvm = execution engine for bytecode.. In practical terms, compare the three components that make java development possible. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the exact steps that take your Java source to a running program. Step one is writing source code in a. java file, typically a class declaration. Step two is compiling that file using the Java compiler, which produces a. class file containing Java bytecode. The command-line flow is simple: run the compiler with the source filename and, if successful, invoke the java runtime with the class name (without the. class extension) to execute it. For example, saving MyFirstProgram. java, running the compiler, and then running java MyFirstProgram produces the console output. A concrete scenario: you type a small class with a main method, you run javac, the compiler reports either success or compilation errors; if success, you run java and the JVM executes the bytecode and shows the printed message.
